III. GEORGE NOELKE’S OBJECTION AND MOTION

        On May 17, 2026, intervenor George Noelke objected to Applicants’ lists of
intervenors who did not file testimony or a statement of position (Objection) and a
motion to provide notice and opportunity for hearing before dismissing intervenors
en masse (Motion).22 Applicants timely filed a response opposing the motion,23 to
which Mr. Noelke replied on May 24.24

          Mr. Noelke argues that Applicants’ lists function as a motion to dismiss that
would strip party status from almost 900 intervenors without adequate notice or a
hearing and violating various rights (e.g., due process25 and the rights under the
Texas Administrative Procedure Act). He stresses that many of these intervenor
landowners—often pro se—were admitted in later orders (SOAH Order Nos. 9, 10,
and 14) that did not restate the deadline in SOAH Order No. 6 to file a position
statement or direct testimony. He also asserts that these intervenors had no actual
notice of the requirement or of their apparent default. Mr. Noelke notes the
Applicants only filed a list, not a proper motion for sanctions under 16 Texas
Administrative Code sections 22.124 and 22.161, reducing their burden while the
ALJs, in every instance, have effectively imposed the harshest sanction sua sponte,
when lesser sanctions were available. Mr. Noelke asks the ALJs to disregard the
Applicants’ list; require the Applicants to file a proper motion to dismiss with real
notice and either a 10-day opportunity to cure or a hearing; order that such notice be
served on each affected intervenor by certified first-class mail with return receipt;
and amend the SOAH Order No. 6 scheduling order so that intervenors’
constitutional and statutory rights are not overridden by 180-day deadline in Texas
Utilities Code section 37.057.


         Applicants oppose Mr. Noelke’s Objection and ask the ALJs to overrule it and
deny his Motion. Applicants make three arguments: First, they complied with
SOAH Order No. 6, which only required Applicants to file a list of non-filing



25 Mr. Noelke cited to and discussed the balancing factors of the Eldridge Test. See Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319,

348 (1976) (establishing a three-part balancing test used to determine if administrative procedures meet the Due
Process Clause of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments).
                                                          8

 intervenors by May 15, 2026—not a motion to dismiss. Applicants timely filed the
list and a corrected version. Applicants argue that SOAH Order No. 6 imposed no
obligation beyond compiling the list, so Mr. Noelke’s “cloaked Motion to Dismiss”
characterization is unfounded. Second, they contend the ALJs may sanction
non-compliant intervenors sua sponte under 16 Texas Administrative Code section
22.161, with no party motion required; adequate notice was already given through
SOAH Order No. 1 and reinforced by Order No. 6’s explicit warning that intervenors
missing the May 13 deadline would be dismissed unless they showed good cause and
requested a hearing by May 20; and 16 Texas Administrative Code section 22.124(a)
authorizes sanctions for missed filing deadlines. Third, they argue that under
16 Texas Administrative Code section 22.104(c), anyone who has filed a motion to
intervene already holds all the rights and obligations of a party while awaiting a
ruling—an instruction repeated in SOAH Order No. 2 and later orders—so those
intervenors were not just permitted but required to file testimony or a statement of
position by May 13 regardless of whether their intervention had been formally
granted.


      Having considered the pleadings, Mr. Noelke’s Objection is OVERRULED
and his Motion is DENIED.
